elements.text: In Silico Modeling of Electro-Exocytosis

How do short electric pulses change
what cells release? How simulation helps predicting it?
Arash Ghorbannia, Ph.D.

notes.text:
SPEAKER SCRIPT

The central question in this project is how very short electric pulses change the particles that living cells release. A higher particle count can have several explanations. Cells may increase regulated vesicle secretion, shed membrane during repair, or release particles as they become injured. Those outcomes have different biological and engineering meanings. We developed a computational framework that follows the response from electrical exposure through the cell and into the surrounding medium, then connects it to the particle assay. In this talk, I will show what we built, the illustrative behavior it produces, and what the preliminary fit to particle measurements can and cannot tell us.

VISUAL CUE
Open with the biological question. Define extracellular vesicles as EVs, then keep the focus on the measured particles.

elements.text: The framework we developed

notes.text: The software uses a reduced, modular description rather than a whole-cell simulation. The eight layers cover electrical dose and membrane response, ion transport and cellular stress, repair, vesicle release, and downstream quality and process outputs. Cell-state modifiers allow us to vary the shared model for different producer-cell settings. The reduced equations carry information from the short pulse into responses lasting seconds to hours. The crucial additional piece is the measurement bridge on the right. Cellular release first enters an extracellular stock, where particles can disappear, and only then passes through an observation model. This keeps secretion distinct from what the instrument reports. Cargo, potency and process outputs remain exploratory model proxies.

title: The fit captures the main particle-size peak

elements.text: The fit captures the main particle-size peak
26 stimulated histograms across three exposure labels and three harvest times
Example: 3 pulses, 40-kV source label
1 h
3 h
Particle diameter (nm)
Blue: observed mean ± sample SD. Pink: fitted model. Vertical axes: 10⁹ particles/mL per bin.
80–380 nm in 20-nm bands.

notes.text: The preliminary calibration uses size-resolved particle measurements from CD4-positive cell preparations. The full dataset has three exposure labels, harvests at half an hour, one hour and three hours, and 26 stimulated histograms. We analyzed fifteen common diameter bands from 80 to 380 nanometers. This slide shows the complete three-pulse condition across all three harvests. Blue points and bars are the observed means and sample standard deviations, and pink curves are the selected fit. The model captures the dominant peak around 100 to 160 nanometers, but it visibly misses part of the one-hour peak. There are three repeated measurements at the outer times and two at one hour. Their biological independence is unknown, and the voltage label is not a confirmed delivered field.

elements.text: Some parameters remain poorly constrained
Exploratory screening and local diagnostics answer different questions
Local information near the fit (excerpt)

All four apoptotic-body parameters
fall below the local information
threshold.

Release scaling, extracellular loss
and assay recovery remain
difficult to separate.
198 runtime parameters and 16 observation parameters screened separately
Dashed line: near-zero-information threshold. Curvature is a local diagnostic, not a confidence interval.

notes.text: We also asked which parameters affect the outputs and which parameters the fitted observations can constrain. Those are different questions. The exploratory sensitivity analysis screened 198 runtime parameters and 16 observation parameters in separate analyses. Source-conversion factors and effective particle persistence can influence the measured concentration. However, near the selected fit, all four apoptotic-body parameters fall below the local information threshold shown here. This is consistent with the limited measurement window and a fitted apoptotic contribution near its lower bound. More broadly, release scaling, extracellular loss and assay recovery remain difficult to disentangle. Recovery was provisionally fixed at one, with uncertainty absorbed into fitted source scales, rather than independently estimated. The analysis guides measurement choices. Its conditional ranges and small sampling design do not justify a definitive biological ranking, and the local curvature is not a confidence interval.

title: The framework makes the next measurements clear

elements.text: The framework makes the next measurements clear
A model for experimental design and further calibration
Exposure and assay controls
Confirm pulse delivery, culture volume and recovery.
Release versus disappearance
Add matched shams and more harvests between 1 and 3 h.
Biological identity and cell state
Pair particle profiles with EV characterization, calcium and injury/viability.
Independent validation
Test the calibrated model on additional exposure conditions.

A working mechanistic framework, a preliminary fit,
and explicit targets for predictive calibration

notes.text: The practical outcome is a clear set of measurements for the next study. First, confirm the delivered pulse and the assay scaling, including medium volume and recovery controls. Second, add matched sham harvests and more observations between one and three hours, so we can better distinguish continued release from disappearance in the medium. Third, combine size profiles with orthogonal EV characterization and measurements of calcium and cell injury or viability. Those measurements connect particle behavior back to the biological pathways. Finally, reserve additional exposure conditions for independent validation. What we have now is a working mechanistic framework and a preliminary observation-level fit. It reproduces the dominant size behavior and exposes the measurements needed to develop a predictive model.
